claim.why_it_matters: Clause depth is the spec's addressing scheme and this file is the citation source of record ('cite the exact §'). Headings one or two levels too shallow break TOC nesting and any ancestry-based navigation: 4.2.5-4.2.7 and 4.2.11-4.2.15 detach from 4.2, 5.2.3-5.2.8 detach from 5.2, and 5.2.6.1-5.2.6.4 (the definitions of brackets, braces and choice indicators) end up at the same rank as 5.2 itself. At '##' these clause headings also collide with the '## Page N' scaffolding rank, so a section can be mistaken for a page marker. Verified against the live file: E:/CobolSharp/specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 2418, 2427, 2436 (4.2.5-4.2.7), 2481, 2486, 2495, 2504, 2513 (4.2.11-4.2.15), 2639, 2644, 2664, 2680, 2683-2698, 2703, 2710, 2726, 2731, 2736-2765, 2783-2803.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED, but the 'kind' label is wrong and the scope is understated. (1) Sources checked independently. Rendered PDF pages 51, 52, 53, 56 and 59 at 200-300 dpi. Page 52 prints exactly three bold headings -- '4.2.5  Implementor-defined language elements', '4.2.6  Processor-dependent language elements', '4.2.7  Optional language elements' -- and page-52.md carries all three with byte-correct titles and complete body text. NOTHING IS MISSING. The 'missing-heading' kind is a misnomer: this is a heading-DEPTH defect, not an omission. (2) The PDF premise is accurate and slightly understated. Below the clause title ('4  Conformance to this Working Draft International Standard', the only visibly larger heading), EVERY numbered heading is set in the identical bold face and size: '4.1  General' and '4.2  A conforming implementation' (p51) are typographically indistinguishable from '4.2.1  General' (p51), '4.2.5' (p52), '4.2.8' (p53), '4.5'/'4.6' (p56) and '5.2.6.1  General' / '5.2.6.4  Choice indicators' (p59). The print carries depth SOLELY in the dotted clause number, never in type size. So the PDF supplies no basis whatsoever for the markdown's varying '#' levels; the transcriber must derive depth from the number. (3) Every cited line number and level in the claim was verified verbatim against E:/CobolSharp/specs/ISO_COBOL.md and all match: 2418/2427/2436 are '## 4.2.5|4.2.6|4.2.7'; 2481/2486/2495/2504/2513 are '## 4.2.11'..'## 4.2.15'; 2564/2571 are '## 4.5'/'## 4.6'; 2639/2644/2664/2680/2703/2710 are '## 5.2.3'..'## 5.2.8'; 2683/2688/2693/2698 are '### 5.2.6.1'..'### 5.2.6.4'; 2726/2731 are '### 5.2.9'/'### 5.2.10'; 2736 '## 5.3' with 2739-2765 '### 5.3.1'..'### 5.3.5'; 2783 '## 5.4' with 2786/2791/2798 '### 5.4.1'..'### 5.4.3'; 2803 '## 5.5'. The named correct siblings also match: 2387/2392/2403/2408 '#### 4.2.1'..'#### 4.2.4', 2446/2451/2456 '#### 4.2.8'..'#### 4.2.10', 2522/2529 '#### 4.2.16'/'#### 4.2.17', 2534/2541 '### 4.3'/'### 4.4', 2589/2599 '### 5.1'/'### 5.2', 2602/2626 '#### 5.2.1'/'#### 5.2.2'. NO MISQUOTE of either source. (4) This is not mere formatting. The single enumerated peer list 4.2.1 through 4.2.17 -- printed as one uniform run in the PDF -- is split across THREE different markdown ranks ('####' for .1-.4, '##' for .5-.7, '####' for .8-.10, '##' for .11-.15, '####' for .16-.17). Direct siblings 4.3/4.4 ('###') versus 4.5/4.6 ('##') are split likewise, as are 5.2.1/5.2.2 ('####') versus 5.2.3-5.2.8 ('##'). Whatever convention one picks, adjacent members of one list cannot legitimately sit at three ranks; the outline this file emits is objectively wrong. (5) The '## Page N' collision is real: line 2413 is '## Page 52' and line 2418 is '## 4.2.5', identical rank; likewise '## 4 Conformance...' (2376) sits at the same rank as third-level '## 4.2.5'. (6) The claim UNDERSTATES the scope, which is the one substantive correction. I tabulated markdown level against clause depth for all 2098 numbered headings in the file: depth-3 clauses appear at '##' 276 times, '###' 508 times and '####' 17 times; depth-4 at '##' 162, '###' 620, '####' 24; depth-5 at '##' 118, '###' 128, '####' 41. Only 59 headings satisfy level == depth+1. There is no consistent convention ANYWHERE in the file -- the 'correct' local pattern ('## 4' / '### 4.1' / '#### 4.2.1') holds only in patches. Nearby examples outside the claimed batch: 2835 '## 5.6', 2840 '## 5.7', 4976 '### 8.1.1', 5079 '## 8.1.3', 5131 '## 8.1.3.2', 5178 '## 8.1.4'. Fixing only pages 51-61 would leave the outline broken; this must be ledgered as a whole-file normalization, not a per-page patch.
verdict.corrected_description: Kind should be 'heading-depth-inconsistency' (or 'wrong-heading-level'), NOT 'missing-heading' -- no heading and no body text is absent from the transcription; every heading on page 52 is present with correct wording. Severity 'structural' is correct. Accurate statement: the ISO PDF sets every numbered heading beneath a clause title in one identical bold face and size (verified on pp. 51, 52, 53, 56, 59 -- '4.1', '4.2', '4.2.1', '4.2.5', '4.2.8', '4.5', '5.2.6.1' are typographically identical), carrying clause depth exclusively in the dotted number. specs/ISO_COBOL.md instead assigns markdown levels arbitrarily, splitting a single printed peer run across two or three ranks: 4.2.1-4.2.4 '####', 4.2.5-4.2.7 '##', 4.2.8-4.2.10 '####', 4.2.11-4.2.15 '##', 4.2.16-4.2.17 '####'; 4.3-4.4 '###' but 4.5-4.6 '##'; 5.2.1-5.2.2 '####' but 5.2.3-5.2.8 '##'. Consequences confirmed: 4.2.5-4.2.7 and 4.2.11-4.2.15 detach from 4.2, 5.2.3-5.2.8 detach from 5.2, 5.2.6.1-5.2.6.4 land at the rank of 5.2 itself, and '##' clause headings tie with the '## Page N' scaffolding and with clause-level '## 4'. The scope is far wider than the claimed p52-p61 batch: across all 2098 numbered headings only 59 satisfy level == depth+1; depth-3 clauses are variously '##' (276), '###' (508) and '####' (17), depth-4 '##' (162), '###' (620), '####' (24), depth-5 '##' (118), '###' (128), '####' (41). Record this as ONE file-wide remediation -- mechanically renormalize every numbered heading to level = (count of dots in the clause number) + 2, so clause '4' -> '##', '4.2' -> '###', '4.2.5' -> '####', '5.2.6.1' -> '#####' -- rather than as a per-page fix, and move the '## Page N' scaffolding off the '##' rank (e.g. to an HTML comment or the existing '<a id="page-N">' anchor alone) so page furniture can never be confused with a clause.
